title: The log rotation that never applied
role: You look after a small Docker host that runs the company API with Docker Compose.

source.label: docker/cli issue #1148: log rotation not working, the container log keeps growing (GitHub)

brief: The disk alert for `docker1.example.com` fires at 96%. Last month Sam added `max-size` and `max-file` to `/etc/docker/daemon.json` and restarted Docker so this would never happen again. It is happening again.

steps.situation: `/var` is almost full and the API still answers, for now. Where is the space going?
steps.evidence:
$ sudo du -xh /var/lib/docker --max-depth=2 | sort -h | tail -3
4.1G  /var/lib/docker/overlay2
38G   /var/lib/docker/containers/3f9c2a
43G   /var/lib/docker
$ sudo ls -lh /var/lib/docker/containers/3f9c2a/
-rw-r----- 1 root root 38G  3f9c2a-json.log

choices.text: Measure /var/lib/docker with du before touching anything
choices.why: One container's `-json.log` is 38 GB. Now you know the fix is about logs, not images or volumes.
It deletes unused volumes, which may hold real data, and every unused image. It doesn't touch the log of a running container, so the disk stays full.

choices.text: Restart Docker to make it rotate
choices.why: Every container stops and starts, and the log file is still there, the same size.

steps.situation: You need space back in the next few minutes. The container is still writing to that file.

choices.text: Empty it in place: truncate -s 0 on the -json.log
choices.why: Docker keeps the file open, so truncating frees the space at once and Docker keeps writing. Copy the last lines elsewhere first if you need them.
The name goes, but dockerd still holds the file open, so `df` doesn't move until the container restarts. `docker logs` also breaks.

choices.text: Stop the API container until you've worked it out
choices.why: It stops the growth, but you've turned a disk warning into an API outage.

steps.situation: Space is back. But why didn't Sam's `daemon.json` limits work?

choices.text: Compare each container's LogConfig with docker inspect
choices.why: The API's config is empty and the newer worker's is not. The settings are there, but only containers created after the change got them.

choices.text: Tell the team that Sam's change broke it
choices.why: Sam's settings are correct. The gap is in how Docker applies them, and blaming people makes them hide the next mistake.

choices.text: Edit daemon.json again and restart Docker
choices.why: Another restart of every container, and the API still keeps the empty config it was created with.

steps.situation: You want the API container to rotate its logs from now on.

choices.text: Add a logging: block in compose, recreate the API in a quiet window, then check inspect
choices.why: Log options are fixed when the container is created. `docker compose up -d --force-recreate api` builds a new one with them. Putting them in the compose file makes the limits travel with the app.
A restart reuses the same container and the same empty config. People in the thread found this out the hard way.

choices.text: Add a cron job that truncates the log every night
choices.why: It keeps the disk alive but throws away each day's logs, so the evidence is gone right when you need it.

debrief.what_happened: In June 2018 a user reported that a container's json-file log grew past 400 MB despite `max-size` and `max-file`. Docker maintainers asked whether the options had actually reached the container, and a maintainer said "You cannot change the configuration for existing containers." Over the next years other users hit the same wall: limits set in `daemon.json` or compose did nothing until the container was recreated, and `docker restart` was not enough. One user showed it with `docker inspect`: the recreated container had the limits, the old one had an empty `Config`. A few reports stayed unexplained, and later docs point to the `local` logging driver.
lessons: daemon.json log options only apply to containers created after the change.
Check what a container really got with docker inspect, not what the config file says.
Truncate an open log, don't rm it: deleted-but-open files keep their space.
Put logging limits in the compose file so they travel with the service.
